archetype.name: Pocket Passer (vertical)
archetype.definition: A rhythm thrower from the pocket who has added real downfield aggression this year, living on intermediate and deep throws rather than his legs.

report.headline: Stroud's new vertical aggression is real; the touchdown rate riding on it isn't.
report.take:
Stroud has always been a pocket passer who wins from structure, and the career line shows how much that depends on the surroundings: a 2023 debut with 8.23 yards per attempt, a 2024 dip to -0.007 EPA per play and a 12-interception season, then a rebound in 2025. This year is a different version of him. His aggressiveness, the share of throws into tight windows, is 20.17% against 12.8% last year, and his intended air yards sit at 9.72. He is throwing into coverage on purpose, and it is paying: throws of 10+ air yards are worth 0.396 EPA each against 0.09 on the short stuff, and the deep ball is returning 0.494 per attempt on 50 tries.

The result is a passer who ranks 13th of 55 in EPA per dropback and 6th in yards a game, carrying an offense whose run game ranks 25th in EPA. The bones of it are sturdy. His sack rate of 4.9% is well under the league's 7.8%, his pressure-to-sack rate has fallen from 30.9% as a rookie to 25.7%, and the line ranks 3rd in keeping him from getting hit. Nico Collins (0.419 EPA per target) and Dalton Schultz carry the volume, and the middle of the field (0.376 EPA per throw) is where he is most dangerous.

What the box score hides is how much of the recent surge is touchdowns. Over the last three games his TD rate is 11%, and on the season 17 of his 22 scores have come in the red zone, where his CPOE is a hot 13.6. Intermediate throws are completed only half the time with a CPOE of -7.1, yet they've produced 9 touchdowns; that's a split built on finishing, not on accuracy. Meanwhile the price of the aggression is creeping in: 3 interceptions in the last three games, a 3% interception rate in that stretch, and 2 lost fumbles that rank 43rd. His CPOE over the last five is just 0.7, well below his season 2.35.

Where it's heading: the downfield approach looks like a real change, not a blip, and protection makes it workable. Expect the efficiency to hold at a good-not-great level, with touchdowns cooling toward two a game and turnovers ticking up as the cost of throwing into tighter windows. The receiving room behind Collins is thinner than the target counts suggest, which caps how high this goes.

strengths.title: Aggressive downfield passing that pays
strengths.body: He's throwing into tight windows far more than last season and the ball beyond 10 yards carries his whole passing game, out-earning the short area by a wide margin. That's a choice backed by a scheme willing to pass more than expected (team pass rate over expected ranks 9th). It's sustainable as a style; the per-play deep numbers will swing with a few completions, but the volume of shots is now part of who he is.

strengths.title: Sack avoidance behind good protection
strengths.body: His sack rate ranks 11th and has dropped to 2.4% over the last five games, while the offense ranks 3rd in hits allowed. His pressure-to-sack rate has improved steadily since his rookie year, so this is part skill trend, part line. It is what lets him hold the ball for 2.92 seconds and wait for routes to develop.

strengths.title: Collins and the middle of the field
strengths.body: Collins turns his targets into 0.419 EPA each, and throws over the middle return 0.376 EPA per attempt with a 55% success rate. That pairing is the most repeatable part of the offense because it rests on a true No. 1 and on Stroud's timing between the hashes, not on scramble plays.

concerns.title: Touchdown rate running ahead of accuracy
concerns.body: An 11% TD rate over the last three games and 17 red-zone touchdowns are carrying the scoring, while intermediate throws are hitting at a -7.1 CPOE. Touchdown share on this kind of volume regresses; the passing yardage, which has been flat lately, is the better guide to what's sustainable.

concerns.title: Turnovers creeping back in
concerns.body: Interceptions have picked up lately, the natural cost of tight-window throws, and his 2 lost fumbles rank 43rd with 3 turnover-worthy fumbles on the season. His 2024 showed what happens when aggressive decisions tip the wrong way, so this is worth tracking rather than dismissing.

concerns.title: Thin help beyond the top options
concerns.body: Xavier Hutchinson has drawn nearly as many targets as Collins but adds almost nothing per target, and throws to the left side are negative in EPA with a -5.5 CPOE. Screens and throws behind the line have cost a lot of EPA, partly a byproduct of a weak run game. With Marvin Harrison Jr. out, more volume could funnel to the least efficient options.

trend.note: After a rough start (negative EPA in Weeks 2 and 3), he has posted double-digit EPA three times since Week 4, peaking at 15.4 against the Chargers; the Cleveland game, where he was blitzed 23 times, is the one recent dip. His EPA per dropback over the last five is well above his season mark, though partly on touchdowns.

nextGame.headline: Ravens' leaky deep secondary, thinned further, sets up Stroud's shot plays
nextGame.body:
Baltimore's pass defense is middling overall (17th) but split in a way that suits him: it's 6th against short throws and 30th against deep ones, and it has been torched by opposing No. 1 receivers (0.72 EPA per target allowed, 31st). That points straight at Collins and at the vertical shots Stroud now takes. The Ravens get to the quarterback often (7th in hit rate) but don't finish (19th in sack rate), which fits a passer who avoids sacks. Houston is a 6.5-point home favorite off 10 days of rest, and his leading-by-9+ EPA (0.343) suggests he stays productive if the game tilts their way, though a lead could also trim his late volume.

Availability favors him. Baltimore is without safety Jaylinn Hawkins (81% of snaps) and defensive tackle Nnamdi Madubuike, and Marlon Humphrey is listed out on a coach's decision with his status unclear; losing a starting safety and possibly a starting corner weakens an already soft deep defense. Lamar Jackson is on IR, which lowers the chance of a shootout that would force Houston to chase. On his side, Harrison Jr. is out, Boutte (hip) is questionable but reportedly not serious, guard Keylan Rutledge (98% of snaps) is questionable with a stinger, and Woody Marks is trending toward returning; Rutledge's status matters most for the interior protection his game depends on.

keyMatchups.title: Deep shots against a bottom-three defense
keyMatchups.body: Baltimore allows 0.847 EPA on deep throws, 30th in the league, and is down a starting safety. Stroud's deep ball has been his most efficient throw. Expect at least a couple of early shots to test the replacement in the back end.

keyMatchups.title: Collins versus Baltimore's WR1 coverage
keyMatchups.body: No defense but one has given up more per target to No. 1 receivers. Collins is Stroud's most productive target by a distance, so the matchup leans heavily his way, especially if Humphrey sits.

keyMatchups.title: The short game won't be free
keyMatchups.body: Baltimore is 6th against short passes, and Stroud's under-10 throws are already his weakest area. If the Ravens take the deep ball away, he'll be stuck in the part of the field where they're strongest.

nextGame.watch: Whether Rutledge plays and holds up inside: clean interior protection is what lets Stroud wait on the deep routes Baltimore can't cover.

restOfSeason.body:
The foundation holds: protection, a lower sack rate, a scheme that leans on the pass, and a quarterback willing to push the ball. That supports yardage around his season norm of the mid-to-high 200s and efficiency in the top third. What won't hold is the recent touchdown pace; a red-zone CPOE in the teens and 9 intermediate touchdowns on 50% completions are finishing luck as much as skill, so expect something closer to 1.6 to 2.4 touchdowns a game. Interceptions are more likely to drift up than down, given how much more often he's throwing into tight windows.

The ceiling depends on the receivers. With Harrison Jr. out, too much volume could go to low-yield options like Hutchinson, while a healthy Boutte and more work for the efficient Jaylin Noel would raise it. A run game ranked 25th means Houston will keep leaning on him, which protects his volume even when efficiency cools.
swingFactors: Health of the receiving corps behind Collins

confidence.note: Ten starts with a clear style change, but deep-ball and touchdown splits rest on small, volatile samples.
